key_facts: Searching algorithms are designed to check for or retrieve an element from a data structure, and are classified into two categories: Sequential Search and Interval Search.
Linear Search starts from the leftmost element of the list, compares the target x with each element one by one, returning the index if matched or -1 if no element matches.
Interval Search algorithms are specifically designed for searching in sorted data structures.
The hash table section covers basic concepts, direct-address tables, hash tables, hash functions, and open addressing as a collision-resolution technique.

The document is authored by Tran Ngoc Bao Duy from the Faculty of Computer Science and Engineering, Ho Chi Minh University of Technology, VNU-HCM, as Chapter 7 of a Data Structures and Algorithms course.
generated_text: Introduction to Searching and Hashing In computer science, efficiently finding and retrieving data is a fundamental task. This lesson introduces two core concepts for this purpose: Searching Algorithms and Hash Tables. We will explore different strategies for searching through data and a powerful technique for mapping keys to values for quick access. Searching Algorithms Searching Algorithms are designed to check for an element or retrieve an element from any data structure where it is stored. Based on the type of search operation, these algorithms are generally classified into two categories. 1. Sequential Search In a sequential search, the list or array is traversed sequentially, and every element is checked. A common example is the Linear Search. Linear Search Approach: Start from the leftmost element of the list and one by one compare the target value x with each element. If x matches an element, return the index. If x doesn’t match any of the elements, return -1. The time complexity of the above algorithm is O(n) . 2. Interval Search Interval search algorithms are specifically designed for searching in sorted data-structures. An example is the Interpolation Search. Interpolation Search Approach: Interpolation Search is an improvement over Binary Search for instances where the values in a sorted array are uniformly distributed. Its approach is as follows: Calculate the value of pos using the probe position formula: pos = lo + ((x - arr[lo]) * (hi - lo)) / (arr[hi] - arr[lo]) arr : The array where elements need to be searched. x : The element to be searched. lo : The starting index in arr. hi : The ending index in arr. If it is a match, return the index of the item, and exit. If the item is less than arr[pos], calculate the probe position of the left sub-array. Otherwise calculate the same in the right sub-array. Repeat until a match is found or the sub-array reduces to zero. Time complexity: If elements are uniformly distributed, then O(log log n) . In the worst case, it can take up to O(n) . Hash Tables Hash tables are a data structure that relies on hash functions to map keys to slots for efficient data retrieval. We will explore one common method for creating these functions. Hash Functions: The Division Method Definition: In the division method for creating hash functions, we map a key k into one of m slots by taking the remainder of k divided by m . That is, the hash function is: h(k) = k mod m Example: If the hash table has size m = 12 and the key is k = 100 , then h(k) = 4. Value of m: When using the division method, the choice of m is important: m should not be a power of 2. m should be a prime not too close to an exact power of 2. Summary In this lesson, we covered the fundamentals of searching and hashing. We distinguished between Sequential Search (like Linear Search) and Interval Search (like Interpolation Search), noting their different approaches and complexities. We also introduced the concept of Hash Tables and explored the Division Method as a technique for creating hash functions, including best practices for selecting the table size m .
